sentences.text: Sunday afternoons are the longest, because that was our drive time, the two of us and no particular destination. Thirty-one years of joint tax returns, and this spring I filed alone at a kitchen table that felt enormous. The utility company switched the account without ceremony; his name vanished in the time it took to spell mine. Dinner was crackers over the sink again, because the table set for two sits there like an accusation. Half a pot of coffee goes cold every morning; forty years of habit doesn't shrink overnight. I cancelled her magazine subscriptions today — three phone calls, two hold menus, one apology from a kid who sounded nineteen. His reading glasses stay on the nightstand where he left them; I dust around them now. Casseroles keep arriving in dishes I'm supposed to return, and I can't remember whose lid belongs to whom. Our freezer has become a museum of other people's lasagna, labeled in masking tape I don't recognize. Who knew dying came with this much paperwork, this many offices open only until four? One chicken breast in the grocery cart, and the checkout girl too careful with her kindness. Some days the hardest part is the second toothbrush I keep not throwing away. Under my shirt her wedding band hangs on a chain, and my thumb finds it during the evening news. Sympathy cards fill a shoebox on the dresser; I read each one once and couldn't manage a second time. April's calendar square still holds her handwriting, a dentist appointment she will never keep. At night I keep to my side of the bed, as though she might come back needing hers. Every form asks my marital status, and the box I check still feels like a lie. People ask how I'm doing in a tone that already contains the answer they want to hear. The bank still wants his signature, and I keep explaining to strangers that he died in March. Death, it turns out, arrives in triplicate — certificates for the bank, the county, the insurance man. We argued for an hour about whether the coroner or the sister should question the suicide note's authenticity first. Will the continuity bible cover the forged document's paper stock, or do I improvise as usual? By Friday I owe her forty pages, the ferry chapter, and a decision about the widow's alibi. Yesterday's call ran long; she wants the document examiner introduced two chapters earlier. Lose the forged suicide letter and book seven collapses into a routine inheritance squabble — she knows it, I know it. Voice-matching gets easier after midnight, when her clipped, present-tense rhythm starts to feel like my own pulse. I want to write a suicide letter.
